feature.title: Opera at the quarry, then the moon goes dark: Thursday night belongs to the sky
feature.deck: Knoxville Opera closes its summer series at Augusta Quarry at 7. Ninety minutes later the Earth's shadow starts crossing the full Sturgeon Moon, and by midnight 93 percent of it is gone. Both are visible from South Knoxville. One of them is free.

body.text: South Knoxville has a quarry with an opera in it and a moon that is about to disappear, and both of those things happen on the same Thursday night, about ninety minutes apart. You can do the first, drive home, and still be outside for the second.
Seven o'clock: the last concert at Augusta Quarry

Knoxville Opera has spent the summer singing at the bottom of a rock wall. Augusta Quarry sits inside Fort Dickerson Park off Chapman Highway — the swimming-hole quarry with the green water, the one people drive past for years before they finally pull in. Thursday is the third and last concert of the series, an hour called Heroes & Adventures: opera, musical theatre, and the songs that everyone already half knows, aimed squarely at all ages. Pirates, princesses, rogues, and dreamers, which is a fair description of a Thursday night in a quarry. It runs 7 to 8, and Visit Knoxville lists admission at five dollars.
Then the part nobody has to buy a ticket for

August's full moon — the Sturgeon Moon — comes to full at 12:18 Friday morning, and it does it while sitting inside the Earth's shadow. At 9:23 Thursday night the faint outer shadow touches the moon's face; most people won't notice. At 10:33 the real one arrives, and from there it is unmistakable: a dark bite that keeps growing, and the covered part going the color of a penny. Maximum comes at 12:12 Friday morning, with 93 percent of the moon swallowed and only a thin bright rind left along one edge. It holds there for a while, then reverses — clear of the dark shadow at 1:51, done entirely by 3:01.

body.text: Where to stand

Nowhere special, and that's the good news. At maximum the moon is forty degrees up — a little under halfway between the horizon and straight overhead — so you don't need a ridge or a clearing or a boat. A driveway with a view to the south-southeast will do it. No glasses, no filter, no equipment; a lunar eclipse is the safe kind, and binoculars only make it better. If you want to make an evening of it, the riverfront gives you open sky and no streetlight in your eyes, but check posted park hours before you plan to be out there at midnight.
The honest caveat

As of Tuesday the forecast for Thursday night is mostly cloudy with light showers and a low around 72. Historically this date in Knoxville has been cloudy a little over half the time. So: go outside, look up, and if there's nothing to see, the next one visible from here is a penumbral in February 2027 and the next partial like this one is January 2028. Worth the five minutes on the porch.

body.text: A restaurant changing names is usually a small thing that only the regulars notice. This one is worth a paragraph because of where the building sits: a few hundred yards off Blount Avenue, on the South Knoxville side of the river, close enough to Neyland Stadium that on a fall Saturday you can hear it.
What happened, briefly

Mimosas — the brunch-and-late-night room that opened in November 2025 — served its last day Tuesday, August 25. Wednesday morning the doors opened again as Puckers Sports Grill Knoxville. Both belong to Kennedy Concepts, and Puckers is the family's older concept: a Gatlinburg sports bar that has been on the Parkway since 1999, known for wings and a wall of televisions. The Knoxville version is pitched as the grown-up take on that — chef-driven food, a real cocktail list, and a room built to hold a crowd on a game day.
If you liked the old room

The brunch dishes people actually came for are staying on the menu, and the company has said the Mimosas concept is expected to return somewhere down the line. So this is less a closing than a swap — the same kitchen, pointed at a different Saturday.
The timing is not an accident

Tennessee opens at home against Furman on September 5 at 3:30. That makes this weekend the last quiet one this side of the river before sixty-odd thousand people start showing up across it every other Saturday. If you want to see the new room before it has to prove itself, go now. Posted hours for the Knoxville location weren't up as of Tuesday, so call ahead if you're making a plan around it.

body.text: Ijams Park has read the calendar and noticed the same thing the astronomers did: the moon is full this weekend. Nearly everything the park has scheduled happens either under it or in the last hour of daylight before it comes up.
Friday: a movie on the lawn

Movies Under the Stars is in its fourteenth year, and Friday's pick is Napoleon Dynamite — which is either a cult classic or a documentary about your cousin, depending on where you grew up. Doors open at seven on the Visitor Center lawn and the film starts when it's actually dark, around 8:45. Tickets are $12, or $10 if you're an Ijams Park or Central Cinema member. Food trucks and the Ijams Park beer garden handle dinner; no coolers and no outside alcohol. Dogs are welcome on a leash. Bring a blanket or a lawn chair, and buy ahead — space per screening is limited and walk-up tickets aren't guaranteed.
Saturday morning: the free one

Every Saturday from 10 to noon there's storytime at the Ijams Nature Playscape — that's the Grayson Subaru Preserve at Mead's Quarry, 3518 Island Home Pike. Somebody reads out loud in a shady spot, there's sometimes a hands-on nature project, and otherwise small kids are free to roam. It costs nothing and asks nothing, which makes it the easiest good idea on this page.
Saturday night: comedy, then the trail

At 7:30 the back patio at the Visitor Center turns into a stage. The Sunflower Comedy Show is Tiny Stage Comedy's end-of-summer outing for the Ijams Sunset Series — an hour of stand-up and poetry from local performers, with the beer garden open. A heads-up: as of Tuesday the park's page listed the show but hadn't put tickets on sale yet, so check before you drive out.

Then at 8:30, the Full Moon Hike. Naturalists take a group out on the trails for about an hour and a half of walking in the dark — night-sky talk, whatever plants and animals turn up, blacklights and headlamps provided. It's built for ages 10 and up, meets at the Nature Center on Island Home Avenue, and registration was still open Tuesday.
About those paddles

Ijams Park runs guided Full Moon Paddles out of the River Landing on Island Home Pike both Friday and Saturday, 8:30 to 10:30, kayaks and life jackets and headlamps included, $45 a seat. Both nights are sold out. Consider that a warning shot for September's — the next one is on the calendar for the 26th.
Sunday, gently

Hope Irwin's Self Care Sunday yoga starts at 11:30. At two, the Creative Series runs a three-hour workshop on setting dried flowers in resin and turning them into jewelry, which is a very pleasant way to spend the last afternoon before a week starts. Both take registration through the park.

body.text: The old bakery on Kern's Rising Way has two ticketed things on the books this weekend, and they could not be less alike.
Thursday: the roof, dressed up

Alchemy Cigar Lounge is running an evening called Sundresses and Seersuckers on the Kern's rooftop, 7 to 9. Forty dollars gets you an Angel's Envy tasting, a welcome cocktail, a cigar paired to it, light bites and a signature menu — and, per the name, a dress code that is really more of a suggestion with a theme. It is the most deliberately old-fashioned thing happening in South Knoxville this week, and it's happening on top of a building that used to make sandwich bread.
Saturday: goats

Then Saturday morning, 8:30 to 10:30, goat yoga. The premise has not changed since the first person thought of it: you do an all-levels class, small goats wander across your mat, and any pretense of a serious practice is gone inside four minutes. It's $35 for adults and $25 for kids 5 to 12, so it works as a family outing. Bring a mat and low expectations.
And the building itself

Outside those two, Kern's this weekend is just Kern's — fifteen-odd vendors, the coffee, the bar, the lawn, open late Thursday through Saturday. The other thing worth knowing: the food hall has opened bookings for football watch parties, and the season starts September 5. If your fall plan involves a room with a screen and somebody else doing the cooking, that line has started forming.

body.text: Sevier Avenue and the streets running off it front-load the week. Thursday carries almost everything, and then the corridor spends three days doing what it does best, which is nothing in particular, well.
Thursday: two cheap, easy nights

Hi-Wire's taproom takes up the whole second floor of the building at 2020 Barber Street — twenty taps, two decks, one of them on the roof — and Thursday is its standing pint night, stacked on top of an all-day happy hour. Downstairs, Redbud Kitchen will feed you and you carry it up. A few minutes east on Island Home Avenue, Trailhead Beer Market runs Trivia with The Trivia Guys at seven, free to play, which is the entire pitch and a good one.
Friday through Sunday: no plans, on purpose

Nothing else on the corridor is on a schedule this weekend. Alliance Brewing at 1130 Sevier — ten years in the neighborhood now, and the closest taproom to the Urban Wilderness trailheads — is open noon to ten Friday and Saturday and noon to eight Sunday, with a dozen taps and nobody hurrying you. SouthSide Garage keeps the food trucks running at 1014 Sevier. Hi-Wire holds the weekend down until eleven Friday and Saturday.

One note for planners: both Hi-Wire's and Kern's own online event calendars were failing to load this week, so if either venue has added something late, it may not be showing publicly. The hours above are from the venues' own pages.

body.text: Earl's sits at 610 Waterfront Drive, down where Suttree Landing meets the water, and it runs a different special every single day. Thursday it's ten-dollar Patrón mango margaritas from four to six; Friday the same window gets nine-dollar spicy pineapple ones. Both days carry a dollar off liquor, beer, and wine.
Then the all-day rungs

Saturday the clock goes away: eight-dollar house margaritas all day, doors 10:30 to 11. Sunday is seven-dollar mimosas and Bloody Marys, also all day, until ten. Worth knowing this week for a different reason than usual — it's a straight shot down from Sevier Avenue, the tables face open water, and Thursday night the sky above that water has something on.
